techniques.name: DeepLIFT
techniques.description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group training a neural network to predict where a regulatory protein binds DNA computes DeepLIFT scores for each predicted binding region against a reference sequence with background base frequencies. They read off which short stretches of bases carry the score, compare them with known binding motifs, and decide whether the model has learned real regulatory sequence before using it to prioritise experiments.

A hospital imaging team is investigating a chest X-ray classifier that flags healthy patients as abnormal. For the false positives it computes DeepLIFT scores against a blurred copy of each image and checks whether the weight sits on the image border, where scanner labels are printed, rather than on lung tissue. It then decides whether to mask the labels and retrain.

A regional geohazard agency uses a neural network to rate landslide susceptibility from terrain, rainfall and land-cover layers. For a slope the model rates as high risk, DeepLIFT scores show which input layers drove the rating, and the agency compares them with the field investigation report before using the map for planning.

A lender's credit team sends each declined applicant a short statement of the factors that most lowered their score. For its neural network scorer it computes DeepLIFT scores against a documented reference applicant, the median approved applicant, and the statement lists the factors with the largest negative scores, which are the ones that pulled this score below the reference.

limitations.description: Every score is relative to a reference input, and the choice changes the picture. In the original paper an all-zero reference on CIFAR-10 images highlighted hard-to-interpret background pixels, while a blurred copy of the image highlighted object outlines. State the reference used and repeat the analysis with at least one alternative before drawing conclusions.

The Captum implementation supports only the Rescale rule, which can give all the credit to one of two inputs that jointly drive the output. In the paper's min(i1, i2) example Rescale scores only the smaller input, while the RevealCancel rule shares the credit. Where inputs interact, the scores can hide a dependency that a more complete rule would show.

Propagation rules must support the network operations. Captum implements the Rescale rule and a limited set of nonlinearities; inaccessible operations in built-in recurrent modules can prevent attribution unless a supported implementation is used.

Two networks that compute exactly the same function can receive different DeepLIFT scores, because differences between a neuron and its reference do not obey the chain rule that gradients obey (Sundararajan et al., 2017, App. B). The scores therefore describe how the model is built as well as what it computes, which matters when comparing a model with a re-implemented or compressed version of it.

Feature contributions account for a particular output difference, not a causal effect in the world or a guaranteed change after deleting that feature. Correlated genomic bases or financial variables make that distinction important.

resources.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
resources.abstract: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. Video tutorial: http://goo.gl/qKb7pL, ICML slides: bit.ly/deeplifticmlslides, ICML talk: https://vimeo.com/238275076, code: http://goo.gl/RM8jvH.

resources.title: An Attribution Deep Learning Interpretation Model for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly used for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) due to their higher accuracy. However, due to the lack of explanations of the influence of input contributing factors by current DL models, accurately identifying the cause of each landslide remains challenging. This study proposes a novel interpretable DL model named Deep-Attention-LSF, which assigns significance scores to contributing factors at local levels for attributing landslide susceptibility. This model considers the significance scores of input factors to more accurately predict landslide occurrence. DeepLIFT is used as an attribution branching network for interpreting the relationship between input factors and each landslide event. Subsequently, a landslide classification network formed by combining convolutional neural network and long short-term memory is used to predict the landslide occurrence in the entire study area. The performance of Deep-Attention-LSF is tested using the landslide inventory map of Three Gorges reservoir area and the associated maps of 18 landslide-related factors. The accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score of our model were 0.9645, 0.9583, 0.9676, and 0.9522, respectively. These suggest that our model outperformed the compared models, including self-attention LSM, frequency-ratio-attention LSM, bagging and random subspace naive bayes tree, gradient boosting decision tree, random forest, information value model and enhanced C5.0 decision tree model. Deep-Attention-LSF provided reasonable explanations for landslide attributions by comparison with field investigation reports for four specific landslide cases. Combining the interpretation of Deep-Attention-LSF with field investigations can provide more comprehensive information for evaluating specific landslides, providing a useful tool for landslide prevention and management.

techniques.name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
techniques.description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

example_use_cases.description: Identifying which pixels in chest X-rays contribute to pneumonia detection, helping radiologists verify AI diagnoses by highlighting anatomical regions the model considers relevant.

A perception team investigating a misclassified traffic-sign image draws the relevance map for the wrong class. The map shows the relevance sitting on a sticker and the background rather than on the sign itself, which tells the team to add training images with such clutter before the model is retested.

A bank's model-risk reviewers receive LRP relevance scores for a sample of declined applications scored by a neural network. They check that the inputs with the most relevance for the decline output are affordability measures and not proxy fields such as postcode, and file the scores with the decision record for audit.

limitations.description: Each layer type needs its own propagation rule, and a new layer type has none until someone derives one, so adapting LRP to a new architecture takes expertise and testing.
Rule selection (LRP-ε, LRP-γ and others) changes the resulting maps, so two analysts can produce different explanations of the same prediction, and choosing among them takes expertise.

Heatmaps are hard to validate. The original paper judges them by eye and with a pixel-flipping test, and notes that quality beyond visual assessment is an open question, so a plausible-looking map does not prove the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Standard rules do not cover attention layers. Extensions for transformers, such as AttnLRP in the LXT library, exist but are recent and specific to certain architectures, so users of transformers or large language models must adopt them and confirm they match their model.

Bias handling and epsilon stabilisation can absorb or inject relevance, so input scores do not always sum exactly to the selected output. A report should document the accounting residual before claiming conservation.

resources.title: On Pixel-Wise Explanations for Non-Linear Classifier Decisions by Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation
resources.abstract: Understanding and interpreting classification decisions of automated image classification systems is of high value in many applications, as it allows to verify the reasoning of the system and provides additional information to the human expert. Although machine learning methods are solving very successfully a plethora of tasks, they have in most cases the disadvantage of acting as a black box, not providing any information about what made them arrive at a particular decision. This work proposes a general solution to the problem of understanding classification decisions by pixel-wise decomposition of nonlinear classifiers. We introduce a methodology that allows to visualize the contributions of single pixels to predictions for kernel-based classifiers over Bag of Words features and for multilayered neural networks. These pixel contributions can be visualized as heatmaps and are provided to a human expert who can intuitively not only verify the validity of the classification decision, but also focus further analysis on regions of potential interest. We evaluate our method for classifiers trained on PASCAL VOC 2009 images, synthetic image data containing geometric shapes, the MNIST handwritten digits data set and for the pre-trained ImageNet model available as part of the Caffe open source package.

resources.title: Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation: An Overview
Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Explaining Deep Neural Network Decisions in MRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks have led to state-of-the-art results in many medical imaging tasks including Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection based on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. However, the network decisions are often perceived as being highly non-transparent, making it difficult to apply these algorithms in clinical routine. In this study, we propose using layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) to visualize convolutional neural network decisions for AD based on MRI data. Similarly to other visualization methods, LRP produces a heatmap in the input space indicating the importance/relevance of each voxel contributing to the final classification outcome. In contrast to susceptibility maps produced by guided backpropagation ("Which change in voxels would change the outcome most?"), the LRP method is able to directly highlight positive contributions to the network classification in the input space. In particular, we show that (1) the LRP method is very specific for individuals ("Why does this person have AD?") with high inter-patient variability, (2) there is very little relevance for AD in healthy controls and (3) areas that exhibit a lot of relevance correlate well with what is known from literature. To quantify the latter, we compute size-corrected metrics of the summed relevance per brain area, e.g., relevance density or relevance gain. Although these metrics produce very individual "fingerprints" of relevance patterns for AD patients, a lot of importance is put on areas in the temporal lobe including the hippocampus. After discussing several limitations such as sensitivity toward the underlying model and computation parameters, we conclude that LRP might have a high potential to assist clinicians in explaining neural network decisions for diagnosing AD (and potentially other diseases) based on structural MRI data.

techniques.name: Taylor Decomposition
techniques.description: Taylor Decomposition explains one prediction of a neural network by splitting its output score into a contribution from each input, such as each pixel. It starts from a reference input, called a root point, that is close to the real input but for which the network's score is zero. Each input's contribution is the slope of the score with respect to that input at the root point, multiplied by how far the input sits from the root, and terms that involve several inputs at once are left out. Finding a good root point is slow for large networks, so the deep variant applies the same idea to one neuron at a time and passes the contributions backwards through the layers, which gives rules close to those of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation. The result is a relevance score for every input that can be drawn as a heatmap.

example_use_cases.description: A quality team uses a convolutional network to flag defective printed circuit boards. For each flagged board they draw the deep Taylor heatmap and check that the highlighted pixels sit on the defect and not on a board label, the edge or the background, before they trust the flags enough to stop manual inspection.

A hospital's model-validation group audits a ReLU network that classifies chest X-rays. For a sample of positive cases, deep Taylor relevance shows whether the evidence for the finding lies inside the lungs or on markers, text or borders added by the imaging equipment, before the group signs the model off for a pilot.

A bank's data science team has a ReLU network that scores small-business loan applications from tabular inputs. For a declined application, deep Taylor relevance lists which inputs supplied most of the score, so a reviewer can see whether the decision rests on repayment history and income or on a field such as postcode.

limitations.description: The explanation depends on the choice of root point, and different reference inputs give different attributions. Finding the nearest root needs an iterative optimisation that is slow for large networks and may not converge, which is why the source applies the deep variant to large image networks.

Plain Taylor decomposition uses only first-order terms, so joint effects of several inputs stay unattributed and the scores need not add up to the prediction. In the source's tests the nearest-root version lost a large share of the relevance, so its heatmaps can leave much of the prediction unexplained.

The deep variant's guarantees, scores that add up to the prediction and are never negative, are proved for ReLU-style layers with zero or negative biases, and iNNvestigate documents support for ReLU networks only. Other activations, positive biases or normalisation layers need workarounds that the proofs do not cover.

Heatmaps explain one input at a time and are hard to validate. The source judges them by eye and by checking that relevance is conserved on MNIST digits and ImageNet photos, so a plausible-looking map does not prove that the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Requires access to internal layer operations and supported redistribution rules. A prediction-only service cannot supply this layer-wise decomposition, and an image-derived rule should not be assumed valid for arbitrary text or attention models.

resources.title: Explaining NonLinear Classification Decisions with Deep Taylor Decomposition
resources.abstract: Nonlinear methods such as Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are the gold standard for various challenging machine learning problems, e.g., image classification, natural language processing or human action recognition. Although these methods perform impressively well, they have a significant disadvantage, the lack of transparency, limiting the interpretability of the solution and thus the scope of application in practice. Especially DNNs act as black boxes due to their multilayer nonlinear structure. In this paper we introduce a novel methodology for interpreting generic multilayer neural networks by decomposing the network classification decision into contributions of its input elements. Although our focus is on image classification, the method is applicable to a broad set of input data, learning tasks and network architectures. Our method is based on deep Taylor decomposition and efficiently utilizes the structure of the network by backpropagating the explanations from the output to the input layer. We evaluate the proposed method empirically on the MNIST and ILSVRC data sets.

techniques.name: Gradient Saliency
techniques.description: Gradient saliency (also called vanilla gradient saliency) is the simplest gradient-based explanation for image classifiers: it takes the gradient of the score for a chosen class (the network's output for that class before it becomes a probability) with respect to every input pixel, in one backward pass, to show which pixels that score is most sensitive to. The gradient says how much the score would change if that pixel changed slightly. The method keeps the size of each gradient and, for colour images, the largest across the colour channels, then shows one value per pixel as a heatmap. Because the sign is dropped, the map shows sensitivity but not whether a pixel supports or counts against the class. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are drawn for the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see whether the sensitive pixels sit on a cue linked to that group; the group-wise errors come from a separate check.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital imaging team validating a pneumonia detection model on chest X-rays computes gradient saliency for a sample of confirmed cases and checks whether the most sensitive pixels lie over the lungs rather than over tubes, monitoring leads or position markers. They use the result to decide whether the model is ready for a clinical pilot or needs retraining on cleaner images.

An agricultural technology company testing a plant disease classifier on leaf photographs taken in the field computes gradient saliency for the images it misclassifies. It checks whether the sensitive pixels sit on the diseased leaf area or on soil, trays and hands in the frame, and decides whether to collect photographs with more varied backgrounds.

A team studying dataset bias fine-tunes an image classifier to separate doctors from nurses in photographs and finds, on a gender-balanced test set, that it errs far more often for one gender. It then inspects gradient saliency on those errors. Where the most sensitive pixels sit on faces and hair rather than on uniforms or equipment, the model is using appearance linked to gender as a shortcut, so the team rebalances the training photographs and retrains.

limitations.description: Maps are noisy and can change sharply for tiny changes to the image, so one map is weak evidence. A study of upper-limb X-ray classifiers found that plain-gradient maps were less accurate at locating abnormalities, and less repeatable, than radiologists' markings (Venkatesh et al., 2024). Look at many images and more than one trained model before drawing a conclusion about the model.

The gradient is local. Where the model's output has flattened, for example once a feature is already strongly present, the gradient is near zero, so a pixel the model relies on can get almost no score. Sundararajan et al. (2017) show this with a one-ReLU example, which is why methods such as Integrated Gradients measure the change from a baseline instead.

Because only the size of each gradient is kept, the map cannot say whether a pixel supports or counts against the chosen class. Evidence that argues against the prediction looks the same as evidence for it, so a map cannot show that a pixel was used in the way a reviewer assumes.

A high score means the output is sensitive to a small change in that pixel, not that the model relied on it or that removing it would change the decision. Pixel-level scores are scattered and often capture only the most discriminative part of an object (Simonyan et al., 2013), so they rarely outline a whole lesion or object a reviewer can name.

resources.title: Deep Inside Convolutional Networks: Visualising Image Classification Models and Saliency Maps
resources.abstract: This paper addresses the visualisation of image classification models, learnt using deep Convolutional Networks (ConvNets). We consider two visualisation techniques, based on computing the gradient of the class score with respect to the input image. The first one generates an image, which maximises the class score [Erhan et al., 2009], thus visualising the notion of the class, captured by a ConvNet. The second technique computes a class saliency map, specific to a given image and class. We show that such maps can be employed for weakly supervised object segmentation using classification ConvNets. Finally, we establish the connection between the gradient-based ConvNet visualisation methods and deconvolutional networks [Zeiler et al., 2013].

resources.title: Gradient-Based Saliency Maps Are Not Trustworthy Visual Explanations of Automated AI Musculoskeletal Diagnoses
resources.abstract: Saliency maps are popularly used to “explain” decisions made by modern machine learning models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). While the resulting heatmaps purportedly indicate important image features, their “trustworthiness,” i.e., utility and robustness, has not been evaluated for musculoskeletal imaging. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of saliency maps used in disease diagnosis on upper extremity X-ray images. The underlying DCNNs were trained using the Stanford MURA dataset. We studied four trustworthiness criteria—(1) localization accuracy of abnormalities, (2) repeatability, (3) reproducibility, and (4) sensitivity to underlying DCNN weights—across six different gradient-based saliency methods (Grad-CAM (GCAM), gradient explanation (GRAD), integrated gradients (IG), Smoothgrad (SG), smooth IG (SIG), and XRAI). Ground-truth was defined by the consensus of three fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologists who each placed bounding boxes around abnormalities on a holdout saliency test set. Compared to radiologists, all saliency methods showed inferior localization (AUPRCs: 0.438 (SG)–0.590 (XRAI); average radiologist AUPRC: 0.816), repeatability (IoUs: 0.427 (SG)–0.551 (IG); average radiologist IOU: 0.613), and reproducibility (IoUs: 0.250 (SG)–0.502 (XRAI); average radiologist IOU: 0.613) on abnormalities such as fractures, orthopedic hardware insertions, and arthritis. Five methods (GCAM, GRAD, IG, SG, XRAI) passed the sensitivity test. Ultimately, no saliency method met all four trustworthiness criteria; therefore, we recommend caution and rigorous evaluation of saliency maps prior to their clinical use.

techniques.name: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
techniques.description: Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) draws a heatmap over an image showing which regions most raise a convolutional neural network's score for a chosen class, which need not be the one the model predicted. The last convolutional layer produces a stack of feature maps, each a coarse grid recording where one learned pattern appears. Grad-CAM takes the gradient of the class score with respect to each map (how much the score changes as that map's values change), averages it to give the map a weight, and adds the weighted maps together. It keeps only the positive values, so the result marks regions that count in favour of the class, then enlarges the coarse grid to the image's size and lays it over the image, so the output shows broad regions rather than pixels. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are laid over the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see which image region the model relies on; the group-wise errors and the training-data counts come from separate checks.

example_use_cases.description: A dermatology AI team validating a melanoma classifier overlays Grad-CAM on dermoscopy images and compares the highlighted region with the lesion outline drawn by a clinician. Cases where the heat falls on a ruler, hair or skin markings are collected, and the team decides whether the training images need cleaning before the model goes to clinical evaluation.

A team developing the traffic sign recogniser for a driver assistance system overlays Grad-CAM on the test images it misclassifies. When the heat sits on the background or a shadow rather than on the sign, they add training images with similar backgrounds and lighting, then recheck the overlays before the release decision.

A team studying dataset bias fine-tunes an image classifier to separate doctors from nurses in photographs and finds, on a gender-balanced test set, that it errs far more often for one gender. It overlays Grad-CAM on those errors: heat on faces and hairstyles rather than on uniforms or equipment shows the model has learned a gender shortcut, and a count of the training photographs by gender shows why. The team rebalances the photographs, retrains and checks that the heat moves.

limitations.description: Needs the network's gradients and its last convolutional feature maps, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an API, or on architectures without convolutional layers. The user must also choose which layer to use, and the paper reports that maps become progressively worse for earlier layers (Selvaraju et al., Sec 3).

The map has the resolution of the last convolutional layer (14 by 14 for VGG-16 and AlexNet), then is enlarged to the image. Small or irregular findings, such as a few-millimetre lesion or a thin sign pole, fall inside one or two cells, so the overlay cannot show whether the model attended to the finding or to its surroundings.

In a chest X-ray benchmark Grad-CAM generally located pathologies better than six other saliency methods but worse than radiologists, with the largest gap for small, complex-shaped findings, and it located them better when the model was confident (Saporta et al., 2022). The overlays are least reliable for the uncertain, hard cases where a reviewer most wants an explanation.

A bright region means features there raise the class score under a local linear approximation, not that the model relied on them. In the paper's own check, Grad-CAM's ranking of image patches agreed only moderately with occlusion, which masks patches and re-scores the image (rank correlation 0.254, Sec 5.3). The ReLU also hides regions that count against the class.

resources.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-based Localization
resources.abstract: We propose a technique for producing "visual explanations" for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models, making them more transparent. Our approach - Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), uses the gradients of any target concept, flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce a coarse localization map highlighting important regions in the image for predicting the concept. Grad-CAM is applicable to a wide variety of CNN model-families: (1) CNNs with fully-connected layers, (2) CNNs used for structured outputs, (3) CNNs used in tasks with multimodal inputs or reinforcement learning, without any architectural changes or re-training. We combine Grad-CAM with fine-grained visualizations to create a high-resolution class-discriminative visualization and apply it to off-the-shelf image classification, captioning, and visual question answering (VQA) models, including ResNet-based architectures. In the context of image classification models, our visualizations (a) lend insights into their failure modes, (b) are robust to adversarial images, (c) outperform previous methods on localization, (d) are more faithful to the underlying model and (e) help achieve generalization by identifying dataset bias. For captioning and VQA, we show that even non-attention based models can localize inputs. We devise a way to identify important neurons through Grad-CAM and combine it with neuron names to provide textual explanations for model decisions. Finally, we design and conduct human studies to measure if Grad-CAM helps users establish appropriate trust in predictions from models and show that Grad-CAM helps untrained users successfully discern a 'stronger' nodel from a 'weaker' one even when both make identical predictions. Our code is available at https://github.com/ramprs/grad-cam/, along with a demo at http://gradcam.cloudcv.org, and a video at youtu.be/COjUB9Izk6E.

resources.title: A Tutorial on Explainable Image Classification for Dementia Stages Using Convolutional Neural Network and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
resources.abstract: This paper presents a tutorial of an explainable approach using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to classify four progressive dementia stages based on open MRI brain images. The detailed implementation steps are demonstrated with an explanation. Whilst the proposed CNN architecture is demonstrated to achieve more than 99% accuracy for the test dataset, the computational procedure of CNN remains a black box. The visualisation based on Grad-CAM is attempted to explain such very high accuracy and may provide useful information for physicians. Future motivation based on this work is discussed.

resources.title: Benchmarking saliency methods for chest X-ray interpretation
resources.abstract: Saliency methods, which produce heat maps that highlight the areas of the medical image that influence model prediction, are often presented to clinicians as an aid in diagnostic decision-making. However, rigorous investigation of the accuracy and reliability of these strategies is necessary before they are integrated into the clinical setting. In this work, we quantitatively evaluate seven saliency methods, including Grad-CAM, across multiple neural network architectures using two evaluation metrics. We establish the first human benchmark for chest X-ray segmentation in a multilabel classification set-up, and examine under what clinical conditions saliency maps might be more prone to failure in localizing important pathologies compared with a human expert benchmark. We find that (1) while Grad-CAM generally localized pathologies better than the other evaluated saliency methods, all seven performed significantly worse compared with the human benchmark, (2) the gap in localization performance between Grad-CAM and the human benchmark was largest for pathologies that were smaller in size and had shapes that were more complex, and (3) model confidence was positively correlated with Grad-CAM localization performance. Our work demonstrates that several important limitations of saliency methods must be addressed before we can rely on them for deep learning explainability in medical imaging.

For the traffic sign recogniser's misclassified test images, the Grad-CAM region falls on the sign face and not the background in all but a reported fraction of cases, and each remaining case has been reviewed

techniques.name: Attention Weight Analysis
techniques.description: Attention weight analysis reads the weights an attention-based neural network assigns to the parts of its input, to see which positions it draws on at each step. The weights come from an ordinary forward pass and are plotted as heatmaps, one row per output step or token. In recurrent encoder-decoder models, such as early neural machine translation or image captioning, each output step has a row over the source words or image regions, read as a soft alignment in which weight is shared across several source positions. In transformers, each attention head (one of several parallel attention units in a layer) has its own matrix at every layer; the analyst views these per head and layer, or averages them over many inputs to profile a head, for example by how much attention it gives each kind of token, or how often its strongest attention lands on a labelled relation such as a verb and its object. The heatmaps show where each step looks; on their own they do not measure how much each input contributed to the prediction, because the weights leave out what is done with the attended values and information mixes between layers.

example_use_cases.description: A localisation team validating an in-house recurrent encoder-decoder translation model for equipment manuals plots the attention matrix for sample sentences and checks that each technical term draws most of its weight from its source counterpart. Sentences whose weight falls mainly on punctuation or the end-of-sentence marker go to a translator; the team first tests this screen on sentences with known errors, and does not treat a clean alignment as proof of a correct translation.

A team assessing an image-captioning model for an alt-text service overlays each generated word's attention weights on the image to check that nouns such as 'wheelchair' or 'crossing' fall on the matching objects. Captions whose nouns attend mainly to background regions are sent for manual review before release, as a screen only: a match does not show that the object produced the word.

A clinical NLP team reviewing a transformer that extracts medication details from discharge letters uses head and model views on a sample of letters to find heads whose attention links each drug name to its dose and frequency, then checks whether those heads behave the same way on letters from a second hospital before describing in the model documentation where those heads look, without claiming that the extraction depends on them.

A model-risk team reviewing a contract-clause classifier uses attention maps as a first look at which phrases the model draws on, then tests the highlighted phrases with an attribution or ablation method before reporting them, because its validation policy does not accept attention weights alone as evidence of what drove a decision.

limitations.description: A bright cell in a heatmap does not show that the input behind it caused the output. In recurrent text classifiers, attention often disagreed with other measures of which words mattered, and very different patterns gave the same prediction (Jain and Wallace 2019). Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) reply that attention can be a believable account without being a faithful one. Neither tested transformers. Confirm any reading by masking the highlighted inputs and checking that the output changes.

In transformers each layer mixes information between tokens, so one layer's weights do not show which inputs a later representation depends on. In a small six-layer transformer, the classification token's weights agreed with deletion-based importance only in the first layer; rollout, which combines weights across layers, agreed better later (Abnar and Zuidema 2020). For a fine-tuned DistilBERT model the gain was small: rollout improves on raw weights but does not fix them.

Each input gives one matrix per head per layer (144 in BERT-base), and the most visible pattern is often uninformative. In BERT, over half the attention in layers 6 to 10 falls on the separator token, which Clark et al. (2019) suggest acts as a 'do nothing' option; Kobayashi et al. (2020) found these weights carry little information once vector size is counted. Profiling a head needs averaging over many inputs, since a few hand-picked examples can mislead.

The weights mean different things in different architectures. In recurrent translation models source attention reads as a word alignment (Bahdanau et al. 2015). In transformer translation models, averaging source attention over all layers gave poor alignments; better ones needed a chosen layer or a measure that counts vector size (Garg et al. 2019; Kobayashi et al. 2020). Check any alignment reading against reference alignments for the model being assessed.

Attention can be trained to look harmless while the model still uses what it hides. Pruthi et al. (2020) trained occupation classifiers to put almost no attention on gender words with little loss of accuracy; the models still used gender, yet reviewers shown the manipulated highlights judged no predictions gender-influenced, against 66% with the original attention. A heatmap showing no weight on a sensitive input is weak evidence; test by changing the input.

resources.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
resources.abstract: Neural machine translation is a recently proposed approach to machine translation. Unlike the traditional statistical machine translation, the neural machine translation aims at building a single neural network that can be jointly tuned to maximize the translation performance. The models proposed recently for neural machine translation often belong to a family of encoder-decoders and consists of an encoder that encodes a source sentence into a fixed-length vector from which a decoder generates a translation. In this paper, we conjecture that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck in improving the performance of this basic encoder-decoder architecture, and propose to extend this by allowing a model to automatically (soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word, without having to form these parts as a hard segment explicitly. With this new approach, we achieve a translation performance comparable to the existing state-of-the-art phrase-based system on the task of English-to-French translation. Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals that the (soft-)alignments found by the model agree well with our intuition.

What Does BERT Look At? An Analysis of BERT's Attention
resources.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

resources.title: Attention is not Explanation
resources.abstract: Attention mechanisms have seen wide adoption in neural NLP models. In addition to improving predictive performance, these are often touted as affording transparency: models equipped with attention provide a distribution over attended-to input units, and this is often presented (at least implicitly) as communicating the relative importance of inputs. However, it is unclear what relationship exists between attention weights and model outputs. In this work we perform extensive experiments across a variety of NLP tasks that aim to assess the degree to which attention weights provide meaningful “explanations” for predictions. We find that they largely do not. For example, learned attention weights are frequently uncorrelated with gradient-based measures of feature importance, and one can identify very different attention distributions that nonetheless yield equivalent predictions. Our findings show that standard attention modules do not provide meaningful explanations and should not be treated as though they do.

techniques.name: Monte Carlo Dropout
techniques.description: Monte Carlo dropout estimates how uncertain a neural network is about each prediction. Dropout randomly switches off some of the network's units and is normally used only in training, but here it stays on at prediction time. Each forward pass (one run of an input through the network) therefore uses a different random pattern of units, and the input is run through typically tens to a hundred times. The average gives the prediction, and the spread across runs is read as epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty from the model's limited knowledge rather than noise in the data. The method approximates Bayesian inference, but the spread is an estimate whose reliability should be checked against held-out errors.

example_use_cases.description: Quantifying diagnostic uncertainty in medical imaging models by running 50+ Monte Carlo forward passes to detect when a chest X-ray classification is highly uncertain, prompting radiologist review for borderline cases.

An autonomous-driving team replays recorded camera footage through its object detector with dropout left on, and finds the scenes (night rain, unusual vehicles) where detections vary most between passes. It uses them to decide what data to collect and which scenarios to add to simulation testing.

A grid operator's demand-forecasting network, trained with dropout, is run 100 times each morning. Days on which the forecasts spread beyond the planners' tolerance are sent for human review before reserve capacity is booked.

limitations.description: The spread across passes reflects uncertainty about the model's parameters, not noise in the data that varies from input to input. An input in a very noisy region can still show a narrow spread, so a narrow spread does not mean the outcome is predictable.

Each prediction needs many forward passes, typically 50 to 100, so inference costs that many times more compute, and too few passes make the spread itself unstable. The passes can run in parallel, which limits added delay but not total compute, so real-time or edge deployments with tight budgets may not afford it.

The network must have been trained with dropout, and the derivation assumes it sits before every weight layer. A model trained without dropout has to be retrained, so the technique is often unavailable for models already built or bought in.

The size of the spread depends on the dropout probability and weight decay, which the developer sets or tunes on validation data rather than learns from the data. The uncertainty scale is partly a design choice and needs checking against held-out errors.

The spread is an approximation, and its behaviour depends on the architecture. In the original paper's regression experiments, uncertainty kept growing away from the training data with ReLU activations but stayed bounded with TanH, so a narrow spread on unfamiliar inputs is not proof of familiarity.

resources.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
resources.abstract: Deep learning tools have gained tremendous attention in applied machine learning. However such tools for regression and classification do not capture model uncertainty. In comparison, Bayesian models offer a mathematically grounded framework to reason about model uncertainty, but usually come with a prohibitive computational cost. In this paper we develop a new theoretical framework casting dropout training in deep neural networks (NNs) as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes. A direct result of this theory gives us tools to model uncertainty with dropout NNs -- extracting information from existing models that has been thrown away so far. This mitigates the problem of representing uncertainty in deep learning without sacrificing either computational complexity or test accuracy. We perform an extensive study of the properties of dropout's uncertainty. Various network architectures and non-linearities are assessed on tasks of regression and classification, using MNIST as an example. We show a considerable improvement in predictive log-likelihood and RMSE compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and finish by using dropout's uncertainty in deep reinforcement learning.

Leveraging uncertainty information from deep neural networks for disease detection
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. While uncertainty is sensitive to clinically relevant cases, sensitivity to unfamiliar data samples is task dependent, but can be rendered more robust.

techniques.name: Temperature Scaling
techniques.description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

resources.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

techniques.name: Monotonicity Constraints
techniques.description: Monotonicity constraints require a model's prediction to move only one way as a chosen input rises, with the other inputs held fixed, so that, for example, predicted salary never falls as years of experience increase. The direction for each constrained feature is set from domain knowledge before training, and the learning algorithm or model structure then rules out any fit that breaks it, so the model cannot learn reversals that come from noise or sampling quirks in the data. Boosted-tree libraries apply the constraint when they choose splits and monotonic neural networks build it into their structure, while penalty-based methods only discourage violations. Because a penalty, a constraint set on the wrong column or a later processing step can still let a reversal through, testers then vary each constrained input across its range over many generated or real cases, with the other inputs fixed, and count any prediction that moves the wrong way. The evidence is that violation count, expected to be zero, together with a comparison of held-out accuracy with and without the constraint.

example_use_cases.description: A mortgage lender constrains its approval model so that higher income, longer employment and a higher credit score can only raise the approval score. Loan officers can then tell an applicant that improving any of these factors can only help the application, and the lender can state each factor's direction to its regulator.

A water utility's pipe-burst risk model is constrained so that risk rises with pipe age and operating pressure and falls with the quality of recent maintenance. Asset managers can then explain the ranked inspection list to the regulator through three directional rules, instead of an opaque score.

A hospital analytics team builds a tree-based model that predicts the cost of care for each patient and constrains the prediction never to fall as age or number of chronic conditions rises. Before release they sweep each constrained feature across its range for thousands of generated patient records, with the other features held fixed, and confirm that no prediction moves the wrong way. They also compare held-out accuracy with and without the constraints.

A utility's day-ahead demand forecast for office buildings is constrained so that predicted demand never falls as occupancy or floor area rises. The validation team writes this as an automated test that draws random building profiles, raises one constrained input at a time and fails the build if any forecast drops, so a retrained model that breaks the rule is caught before deployment.

limitations.description: Forces a one-way relationship even where the real one reverses, such as an inverted U between experience and performance. The model then fits that feature worse and cannot show the turning point, so held-out accuracy should be compared with and without the constraint.

Choosing which features to constrain, and in which direction, needs domain expertise. A wrong constraint builds a false belief into the model, and the check on the trained model will still pass, because it shows only that the constraint holds, not that it is right.

The rule covers one feature with the others held fixed, and says nothing about the size of the effect. A model can meet it by ignoring the feature, and when correlated inputs move together a person's overall score can still fall as one favourable input rises, so the constraint does not make the whole model easy to explain.

Support differs by model family. Tree-boosting libraries such as XGBoost accept constraints directly, while neural networks need a special architecture or a penalty term. With histogram-based tree methods, constraints can remove every candidate split and leave shallow trees that underfit.

A sweep or property-based test samples the input space. It can find a violation but cannot prove there is none, and a pass depends on how well the generated inputs cover realistic and rare combinations of features.

However, when statistical data are used in supervised training of a neural network employing the back‐propagation least mean square algorithm, the behavior of the classification boundary during training is often unpredictable. This research suggests the application of monotonicity constraints to the back propagation learning algorithm. When the training sample set is preprocessed by a linear classification function, neural network performance and efficiency can be improved in classification applications where the feature vector is related monotonically to the pattern vector. Since most classification problems in business possess monotonic properties, this technique is useful in those problems where any assumptions about the properties of the data are inappropriate.

resources.title: An informed monotone neural network for multi-stage chronic kidney disease prediction with integrated GFR estimation
resources.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive condition affecting over 850 million people worldwide, where timely detection and accurate staging are critical to reducing morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Current machine learning approaches often treat CKD prediction as a binary task, neglecting the ordered nature of disease stages, and rarely incorporate physiological constraints or calibrated probability estimates essential for clinical decision support. We propose a multi-stage CKD prediction framework that integrates ordinal classification, probability calibration, and a serum creatinine-monotonicity constraint within a knowledge distillation paradigm. A calibrated CatBoost model serves as a teacher, transferring temperature-scaled class probabilities to an ordinal neural network student augmented with an auxiliary eGFR regression task. Evaluated on a cohort of 750 patients from Al-Ramadi Teaching Hospital, our approach achieved superior macro-F1 and reduced expected calibration error. This work demonstrates that combining ordinal learning, calibration, and physiological constraints yields models that are not only accurate but also aligned with clinical reasoning, offering a pathway toward safer and more trustworthy AI tools for CKD management. Limitations like circular reasoning and target leakage are also discussed.

techniques.name: Neuron Activation Analysis
techniques.description: Neuron activation analysis examines when individual neurons in a neural network respond strongly. The analyst runs a set of inputs through the model, finds the inputs that activate a chosen neuron most and least, and looks for the concept that separates them, such as buildings in an image classifier or French text in a language model. Some methods test the match automatically, for example by scoring how closely a neuron's activation lines up with labelled examples of a concept. The result is a list of neurons with candidate meanings and the evidence behind each. These meanings are correlations between inputs and activations, so they show what a neuron responds to, not what it does to the model's output.

example_use_cases.description: An ML team inspects a scene classifier trained to sort building and street images. For each neuron in a late layer they compare the images that activate it most with those that do not, using object labels from the dataset. Some neurons line up with a clear concept such as a building and others only weakly, which tells the team how much of the layer can be read.

A hospital assurance team examines a clinical language model and finds neurons whose strongest activations come from text about a particular drug class or condition. A clinician reviews whether the concepts are the expected ones. The finding shows which clinical concepts the model represents internally, not that these neurons cause any particular suggestion.

limitations.description: Many neurons respond to several unrelated concepts, or play different roles depending on the surrounding input. A single label such as 'toxic language' can then be wrong or only part of the story, and consistent interpretation across scenarios is hard.

Behaviour is often spread across many neurons instead of held in one, so a neuron-by-neuron view can miss it. Checking combinations of neurons is much harder than checking single ones, and the number of combinations grows quickly.

The analysis shows which inputs make a neuron fire, not what the neuron contributes to the output. Showing that a neuron matters needs a separate experiment that switches it off or alters it and measures the effect.

A neuron can only be matched to concepts the analyst has examples for. In image models this means a densely labelled dataset, and a neuron whose concept is missing from it goes unexplained or is mislabelled.

The method needs access to the model's internal activations, so it cannot be used on a model reached only through an API. Large language models have hundreds of thousands of neurons or more, so in practice only a chosen subset can be examined and labelled with care.

resources.title: On the Value of Labeled Data and Symbolic Methods for Hidden Neuron Activation Analysis
resources.abstract: A major challenge in Explainable AI is in correctly interpreting activations of hidden neurons: accurate interpretations would help answer the question of what a deep learning system internally detects as relevant in the input, demystifying the otherwise black-box nature of deep learning systems. The state of the art indicates that hidden node activations can, in some cases, be interpretable in a way that makes sense to humans, but systematic automated methods that would be able to hypothesize and verify interpretations of hidden neuron activations are underexplored. This is particularly the case for approaches that can both draw explanations from substantial background knowledge, and that are based on inherently explainable (symbolic) methods.   In this paper, we introduce a novel model-agnostic post-hoc Explainable AI method demonstrating that it provides meaningful interpretations. Our approach is based on using a Wikipedia-derived concept hierarchy with approximately 2 million classes as background knowledge, and utilizes OWL-reasoning-based Concept Induction for explanation generation. Additionally, we explore and compare the capabilities of off-the-shelf pre-trained multimodal-based explainable methods.   Our results indicate that our approach can automatically attach meaningful class expressions as explanations to individual neurons in the dense layer of a Convolutional Neural Network. Evaluation through statistical analysis and degree of concept activation in the hidden layer show that our method provides a competitive edge in both quantitative and qualitative aspects compared to prior work.

resources.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
resources.abstract: We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN model, the proposed method draws on a data set of concepts to score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer. The units with semantics are labeled across a broad range of visual concepts including objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the hypothesis that interpretability is an axis-independent property of the representation space, then we apply the method to compare the latent representations of various networks when trained to solve different classification problems. We further analyze the effect of training iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, and measure the effect of dropout and batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative power.

Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
resources.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

sample_claims.text: For each sampled neuron in the clinical language model, the concept that best explains its strongest activations is recorded with a match score, and neurons below the agreed score are reported as not interpreted.
The concept labels assigned to the classifier's late-layer neurons hold on held-out images: the labelled neurons activate far more strongly on images of the concept than on images without it.
The language-model analysis documents the contexts producing high and low activation for each selected unit.

techniques.name: Causal Mediation Analysis in Language Models
techniques.description: Causal mediation analysis traces which internal components of a language model carry the effect of a change in the input to the output. The analyst makes a controlled change to the input, such as swapping 'nurse' for 'man' in a prompt, and measures how the model's next-word probabilities shift. To find the indirect effect through one component (a single neuron, or an attention head, which is the part of the model that chooses which earlier words to focus on), they feed the model the original input but give that component the value it took on the changed input. To find the direct effect, they feed the changed input but hold that component at its original value. Repeating this across many components shows where in the network a behaviour is carried.

example_use_cases.description: A safety team finds that a language model gives unsafe medical advice when a request is phrased as an instruction rather than a question. They compare outputs for the two phrasings and use mediation analysis to find which attention heads carry most of the shift in the probability of the unsafe reply, so a fix can target those heads and the analysis can be rerun to check it worked.

A research team studying why a language model sometimes gets subject-verb agreement wrong in sentences with an intervening clause changes the number of the subject noun and measures the shift in the verb's probability. Mediation analysis then shows which neurons carry the number information, and whether the same neurons are used across sentence structures.

limitations.description: Needs white-box access and knowledge of the architecture. The analyst must read and overwrite activations at chosen points inside the model, so it cannot be used on a model offered only through an API, and a poorly chosen intervention point can give misleading conclusions.

Conclusions hold for the contrast tested. Swapping 'nurse' for 'man' and tracking one probability ratio tests a single contrast, and a different prompt set or outcome measure can point to different components. Effects also differ between models: larger GPT-2 models showed larger effects, and masked language models matched less well.

Every component and every prompt needs its own forward passes, so testing all the neurons or heads of a large model on many prompts is expensive. Analysts often test a subset or groups of components, which can miss effects elsewhere in the network.

Single-component effects do not simply add up. Vig et al. found that intervening on all neurons together produced an effect far larger than the sum of the single-neuron effects, so ranking components one at a time can understate or misplace where a behaviour is carried.

The split into direct and indirect effects is not guaranteed to be exact. In a non-linear network the total effect need not equal their sum, and Vig et al. report only an approximate match for GPT-2, so the split should be checked rather than assumed.

resources.title: Investigating Gender Bias in Language Models Using Causal Mediation Analysis
resources.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

resources.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language Models
resources.abstract: Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate the magnitude of models’ preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across architectures and model sizes—notably, that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.

techniques.name: Concept Activation Vectors
techniques.description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

example_use_cases.description: Auditing a medical imaging model to check whether its chest X-ray classifications are sensitive to diagnostic concepts (like 'tumour characteristics') or to irrelevant ones (like 'scanner type' or 'patient positioning'), so the clinical team can judge whether the model relies on medically relevant information.

A team auditing an image classifier used for content tagging builds concept sets from photographs of people of different ethnicities and genders, with random photographs as the comparison, and tests each output class for significant sensitivity to those concepts, as the original paper did. Classes with significant sensitivity to an ethnicity or gender concept are listed for retraining with balanced data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A developer of a driver-assistance system documents, for a type-approval authority, how its traffic-sign classifier responds to visual concepts. The report gives significance-tested TCAV scores for the 'stop sign' class against concepts such as graffiti, snow cover and low sun glare, so the authority can see what the classifier's predictions are sensitive to.

limitations.description: Requires clearly defined concept examples and non-concept examples, which can be hard to obtain for abstract or subjective concepts. If the examples differ from the random counter-examples in other ways, such as image source or lighting, the CAV mixes those differences in with the concept.

Assumes the concept is represented as a direction that a linear classifier can pick out at the chosen layer. If the concept is not linearly separable there, the CAV is unreliable, so check that the classifier separates the two sets well before reading any scores.

Results depend heavily on which layer is examined, because layers capture different levels of abstraction. A concept can be invisible at one layer and strong at another, so a single-layer result should not be generalised.

The significance test trains hundreds of classifiers per concept and layer (the paper uses about 500), so cost multiplies with the number of concepts and layers tested. FastCAV, a 2025 preprint, reports speed-ups of up to 63.6 times.

Scores are class-level and describe sensitivity, not cause. A TCAV score is the share of a class's inputs whose score rises along the concept direction, so it does not explain an individual decision, and a high score does not show that the concept causes the prediction.

resources.title: FastCAV: Efficient Computation of Concept Activation Vectors for Explaining Deep Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Concepts such as objects, patterns, and shapes are how humans understand the world. Building on this intuition, concept-based explainability methods aim to study representations learned by deep neural networks in relation to human-understandable concepts. Here, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) are an important tool and can identify whether a model learned a concept or not. However, the computational cost and time requirements of existing CAV computation pose a significant challenge, particularly in large-scale, high-dimensional architectures. To address this limitation, we introduce FastCAV, a novel approach that accelerates the extraction of CAVs by up to 63.6x (on average 46.4x). We provide a theoretical foundation for our approach and give concrete assumptions under which it is equivalent to established SVM-based methods. Our empirical results demonstrate that CAVs calculated with FastCAV maintain similar performance while being more efficient and stable. In downstream applications, i.e., concept-based explanation methods, we show that FastCAV can act as a replacement leading to equivalent insights. Hence, our approach enables previously infeasible investigations of deep models, which we demonstrate by tracking the evolution of concepts during model training.

resources.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
resources.abstract: The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size, complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net’s internal state in terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important to a classification result–for example, how sensitive a prediction of “zebra” is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a medical application.
